en: Now, the beginningless impurity (anādimala) of persons is proclaimed as their state of bondage (paśutva);
it should be understood as being like the husk and the chaff of a sprout emerging from the seed-vessel of Māyā. ||1||
The flood of human fetters, beginning with ignorance, exists under the power of that [mala].
Therefore, one who desires imperishable liberation must know that reality according to its true nature. (2)
That [Self] is accessible solely through the knowledge of the Lord and is not within the range of others;
therefore, one whose self is purified by those who know Him is called "liberated" by the wise. (3)
If impurity does not belong to the person, then by what is attachment to enjoyments produced?
O wise one, for a pure person, such enjoyment is simply impossible.
Furthermore, if enjoyment were logical, that logic would not be tenable,
because there would be no perceived distinction between one who is liberated and one who stands on the path of saṃsāra.
Therefore, a specific distinction consisting of the nature of the person (puruṣa) must be accepted, in the absence of which neither the liberated self nor the bound self could be postulated. (6)
All states of being that arise from that [consciousness] belong to the nature of illusion for the bound soul;
they accomplish here the two-fold human goal, both higher and lower. (7)
The principle of Māyā is the seed of the universe, indestructible, and of the nature of Śiva;
it is all-pervading, one, partless, subtle, beginningless, imperishable, and sovereign.
Therefore, O Kālakalā, from Rāga and Vidyā [proceeds] the Manifest (Vyakta); from the Guṇas, Intellect (Dhī);
from the principle of Intellect (Buddhitattva), Ego (Ahaṃkāra), the subtle elements (Tanmātras), and the sense organs (Indriyas). || 9 ||
And from the subtle elements (tanmātras), he— Śiva, the Lord of the lords of knowledge and ignorance, empowered by Śiva’s power— gradually created the gross elements and everything else.
That Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, created all things— the principles of existence, the products of the creative intellect, the elements, and the worlds— the entire universe consisting of māyā.
The transformation of this world, consisting of the three guṇas, arises from karma; it is therefore composed of the peaceful, the terrible, and the deluded, and is exceedingly diverse.
And from karma come the various bodies of embodied beings;
from karma comes this entire fruit consisting of pleasure and pain. 13.
Having obtained bodies as individual souls (aṇu), they repeatedly perform actions;
their selves are possessed by the state of being bound (paśutva), and their minds are overwhelmed by worldly enjoyments. || 14 ||
If those two did not exist, bondage and liberation would never occur for men;
yet they do indeed occur for you, based on valid cognition and realization. (15)
When these—impurity, action, and the state of being Śiva—are present, there arise these three purposes of the world's creation: experience, the state of being an enjoyer, and liberation. (16)
The karma of the bound soul (paśu) consists of two kinds: that which is to be experienced, and that which is of the nature of merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma).
It is of these two kinds;
it is of these two kinds.
One should know that it persists through application and is opposed to the two types of results. || 17 ||
It sustains all these worlds and brings supreme joy to man;
therefore, it is called Dharma by those who know it, and Adharma is its opposite.
The realization of the means for accomplishing dharma arises from the sacred tradition (āmnāya) alone;
and because the Smṛti is rooted in that [tradition], as well as the other [Dharmaśāstras], it too arises from those two alone. || 19 ||
Just as the rising and falling of the two ends of a balance scale occur simultaneously,
so too do the dissolution of a past action and the arising of a future one.
The state beginning with non-attachment and ending with liberation is called the bondage of the soul due to the obstruction of the two-fold karma; it brings about the cessation of perfect isolation.
The innate (nija) agency of the Person is beginningless, ending in liberation, and unchanging;
however, that which belongs to Māyā and that which belongs to Karma do not end in liberation, because they are of a different nature.
This illusion consists of the individual soul and karma; such is the subtle bondage.
All this has been told by me in brief, O son of Kaśyapa. 23.
Therefore, initiation alone liberates one from that extensive bondage which obstructs the supreme state, and leads [the soul] upward even to the abode of Śiva.

For one who has dedicated himself to the abode of Śiva and is an enjoyer of worldly experience, there is never again the state of being an enjoyer, nor the status of an office-holder, nor the imitation of the duties of a husband. (25)
Having transcended the state of arising from existence, he stands like an unshakable flame;
since his nature as Śiva has become manifest, he is liberated and has accomplished all that was to be done. || 26 ||
Thus ends the second chapter, concerning the investigation of bonds, in the Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṅgraha.
